Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:10:1.hebrew: תצא מעצמה - משמע, וליכא לאוקמי קרא כשהדליק הוא עצמו גדישו של חבירו, אלא בתוך שלו הדליק והאש הלכה מעצמה. ואפילו הכי קרי מבעיר את הבערה כאילו הדליקו בעצמו, אלמא אשו משום חציו:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:10:1.english: Breaks out on its own - [this is what the verse] implies, and one cannot interpret the verse [as referring to a case] where he himself ignited his fellow's grain stack; rather, he ignited [it] within his own [property] and the fire went on its own. And even so, [the verse] calls [him] "the one who ignited the fire," as if he had ignited it himself; thus, [liability for] his fire is due to [its similarity to] his arrows.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:1:1.english: To overload - his camel with a load until it enters into the store.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:1.english: And there was a kid tied to it - To the stack.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:2.english: And a slave adjacent to it - To the stack.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:3.hebrew: ונשרף עמו חייב - אגדי ואגדיש, לפי שאין לו דין מיתה בשביל העבד, שהיה לו לברוח:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:3.english: And [the slave] was burned with it, he is liable - [He is liable] for the goat and for the stack, because he is not subject to the death penalty on account of the slave, since [the slave] should have fled.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:4.hebrew: עבד כפות לו וגדי סמוך לו ונשרפו עמו פטור - אגדי ואגדיש, דקם ליה בדרבה מיניה, שההורג העבד נהרג, דכתיב: "נקם ינקם" (שמות כ״א:כ׳). והאי דנקט גדי, משום דמוקמינן לקמן בגדי דחד ועבד דחד, דבגדיש ועבד ליכא לאוקמי הכי, דאורחא דמלתא לשדורי איניש עבדיה לשמור גדישו. ואיידי דנקט גבי עבד כפות וסמוך, נקט גבי גדי כפות וסמוך; ואע"ג דבגדי אין לומר "היה לו לברוח", שהרי אין בו דעת, ואם אינו כפות וסמוך נמי חייב, כדאמרינן בשילהי פרקין (דף כז.): "שורו כממונו":
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:2:4.english: [If a] slave was tied to it and a goat was adjacent to it, and they were burned with it, he is exempt - [He is exempt from paying] for the goat and for the stack [of grain], because he is subject to the greater [punishment] than it, for one who kills a slave is executed, as it is written: "He shall surely be avenged" (Exodus 21:20). And the reason [the Mishnah] specifically mentions a goat is because we establish later [in the Gemara] that [the case involves] a goat belonging to one [person] and a slave belonging to another [person]; for regarding the stack [of grain] and the slave, it is not possible to establish it thus, since it is the normal way of things for a person to send his slave to guard his [own] stack [of grain]. And since [the Mishnah] stated "tied" and "adjacent" with respect to the slave, it [also] stated "tied" and "adjacent" with respect to the goat, even though regarding a goat one cannot say "it should have fled," because it has no intelligence, and even if it is not tied [but merely] adjacent, he is also liable, as we say at the end of our chapter (27a): "His ox is like his property."

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:3:1.hebrew: אם קטל תוריה עבדא ה"נ דלא ליחייב - ממון? הא כתיב: "כסף שלשים שקלים יתן לאדוניו" (שם):
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:3:1.english: If his ox killed a slave, would he also not be liable - [for] monetary compensation? Behold, it is written: "Thirty shekels of silver he shall give to his master" (ibid. [Exodus 21:32]).

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:4:1.english: That he set fire to the body of the slave - For he certainly actually killed him.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:5:1.hebrew: בגדי דחד ועבדא דחד - ואיצטריך לאשמועינן דאע"ג דאין חייב מיתה בשביל הגדי, מפסיד בעל הגדי:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:5:1.english: With a goat of one [person] and a slave of another - And it was necessary to teach us that even though he is not liable to the death penalty on account of the goat, the owner of the goat loses [his compensation].

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:7:1.hebrew: אילו מסר שורו לחרש ה"נ דלא מיחייב - הא אמרינן בפ"ק (ד' י.), חומר בשור מבאש, שאם מסרו לחרש — חייב:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:7:1.english: If he were to convey his ox to a deaf-mute, would he also not be liable - Surely we stated in the first chapter (10a) [that there is] a stringency in [the case of] an ox over [the case of] fire, that if he conveyed it to a deaf-mute, he is liable.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:8:1.hebrew: גחלת וליבה - החרש, דלא דמי לשור, דשור מזומן להזיק; אבל הא דגחלת, חרש עביד ליה להיזק:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:8:1.english: A coal and he fanned it - [Meaning] the deaf-mute [fanned it], for [this] is not similar to an ox, since an ox is poised to cause damage; whereas [in] this [case] of a coal, the deaf-mute brings about the damage.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:8:2.english: The damage is certain - Its damage is imminent, and it is like his ox.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:9:1.hebrew: ור' יוחנן אמר אפילו שלהבת פטור - ור' יוחנן לטעמיה, דאמר אשו משום חציו, והכא חציו דחרש הן:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:9:1.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said: Even [for] a flame he is exempt - And Rabbi Yochanan [follows] his [own] reasoning, as he says [that] one's fire [is liable] due to [its being like] his arrows, and here they are the deaf-mute's arrows.

Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:9:3.hebrew: וסילתא - עצים קטנים דקים, דהאי ודאי פושע הוא:
Rashi on Bava Kamma 22b:9:3.english: And kindling chips - Small, thin pieces of wood, for this [person] is certainly negligent.

Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:1:1.hebrew: רישא בעל גמל חייב וכו' - אע"ג דמעיקרא נמי הוי טעמא דרישא וסיפא הכי, אלא דמעיקרא היה הטעם פשוט יותר למאן דאמר אשו משום חציו, דמתחייב בעל הגמל על תחלת הדלקת הפשתן, ואע"פ שהאש הולכת מעצמה ע"י רוח מצויה; אבל למ"ד משום ממונו, דלא מחייב אלא על שמסכסכת הבירה, ובזה לא פשע כ"כ — שלא ראה הדליקה עד שעמדה סמוך לבירה, ואז לא היה יכול לסלקה לפי שעמדה להטיל מימיה — ולכך הוצרך לפרש דאפ"ה חייב, דלא איבעי ליה לאפושי בטעיניה, דהוה ליה לאסוקי אדעתיה כשיכנס פשתנו לתוך החנות ותדליק בנר ותעמוד להטיל מימיה, לא יוכל לסלקה משם:
Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:1:1.english: In the first clause, the owner of the camel is liable, etc. - Even though originally as well the reason for the first clause and the latter clause was thus, nevertheless originally the reason was more straightforward according to the one who says [that liability for] one's fire is due to [it being considered] one's arrows — for the owner of the camel becomes liable for the initial ignition of the flax, even though the fire spreads on its own through an ordinary wind. However, according to the one who says [that liability for fire is] due to [it being] one's property — where he is only liable for [the fact] that it [the camel] ignites the building, and in this [regard] he was not so negligent, since he did not see the fire until [the camel] stood next to the building, and then he could not remove it because it stood [still] to urinate — therefore [the Gemara] needed to explain that even so he is liable, because he should not have overloaded [the camel], for he should have considered that when his flax enters into the store and catches fire from the lamp, and [the camel] stands [still] to urinate, he will not be able to remove it from there.

Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:2:1.hebrew: והיה גדי כפות לו - תימה, דליתני ברישא גדי ועבד סמוך, ובסיפא גדי ועבד כפות, דהוי רבותא טפי! ופי' רשב״ם, דגדי נמי היה לו לברוח, ורישא דקתני גדי כפות ועבד סמוך — דוקא בכה״ג חייב. ובסיפא "גדי סמוך ועבד כפות לו" — פי': או עבד כפות לו; וה״פ: גדי סמוך לו ועבד כמו שאמר ברישא, שהיה סמוך לו — פטור, אע״ג דלא קם ליה בדרבה מיניה, משום דהיה לו לברוח; ועבד כפות לו, וגדי כמו כן כפות כמו שאמר ברישא — פטור, אע״ג דלא היה לו לברוח, דקים ליה בדרבה מיניה. וההוא דסוף פירקין (בבא קמא ד' כז.): "עבדו כגופו, שורו כממונו" — איירי בעבד ושור כפות והבעלים עומדים אצלם, וכשהניח הגחלת על לב עבדו פטור, שמחשב בלבו שהאדון יסירנה ולא יסמוך אתשלומין; אבל כשהניח על לב שורו, אינו חושש האדון להסירה, לפי שישלם לו דמי שורו. ור״ת מפרש דאיצטריך "גדי כפות" דחייב, אע״ג דפטרינן טמון באש, דדרשינן: מה קמה בגלוי, אף כל בגלוי, וס״ד דכל דבר דלאו אורחיה הכי לאו כעין קמה הוא ופטור, וגדי אין דרכו להיות כפות, וס״ד למפטריה — וקמ״ל השתא ברישא דאפ״ה חייב. וסיפא קמ״ל דאע״ג דסמוך הוא, דהוי כי אורחיה, פטור. לכך תניא ההיא מתניתין דהכונס (לקמן בבא קמא דף סא:) בתר פלוגתא דטמון דר' יהודה ורבנן, ובתר הך בבא דגדי כפות קתני: "ומודים חכמים לר' יהודה במדליק הבירה שמשלם כל מה שבתוכה, שכן דרך בני אדם להניח בבתים"; והפסיק התנא בהאי בבא כדפרישית, לאשמועינן דאע״ג דלאו אורחיה בגדי להיות כפות — חייב. ואפילו למ״ד אשו משום חציו, דלא שייך בדידיה למפטר טמון, מ״מ אצטריך לאשמועינן דחייב היכא דכלו לו חציו לאחר שריפת העבד; ואע״ג דשריפת העבד מחמת חציו ושריפת גדי מחמת ממונו, שייך ביה שפיר קם ליה בדרבה מיניה, הואיל וע״י מעשה אחד בא הכל. ותדע, דלמ״ד משום ממונו מוקי כשהצית בגופו של עבד, ופטרינן ליה אע״ג דלא הצית בגופו של גדי. ולפי' ר״ת ורשב״ם אתי שפיר הא דנקט גדי ולא נקט גדיש. ובקונטרס פי', משום דמסקינן בגדי דחד ועבדא דחד, וסתמא העבד לבעל הגדיש, שאדם מניח עבדו לשמור גדישו; ולפירושו צ״ל: הא דפריך "מאי למימרא", הוה מצי למימר "ולטעמיך תיקשה לר' יוחנן אמאי נקט גדי":
Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:2:1.english: And there was a goat tied to it - It is astonishing: [why did the Mishnah not] teach in the first clause [that] a goat and a slave were adjacent [to it], and in the latter clause [that] a goat and a slave were tied [to it], for that would be a greater novelty! And Rashbam explained that a goat too should have fled, and [therefore] the first clause, which teaches "a goat tied and a slave adjacent," [means that] specifically in such a case is he liable. And in the latter clause, "a goat adjacent and a slave tied to it" — [the] explanation [is]: "or a slave tied to it"; and this is its explanation: [if] a goat is adjacent to it and a slave, as it said in the first clause, was [also] adjacent to it — he is exempt, even though he does not receive the greater penalty, because [the goat] should have fled; and [if] a slave is tied to it, and a goat is likewise tied as it said in the first clause — he is exempt, even though [the goat] could not have fled, because he receives the greater penalty. And that [passage] at the end of our chapter (Bava Kamma 27a), "[if one places a coal on] his slave, [it is] like [on] his own body; [on] his ox, [it is] like [on] his property," speaks of a tied slave and ox with the owners standing beside them; and when he placed the coal on the heart of his slave he is exempt, because he thinks in his heart that the master will remove it and will not rely on payment; whereas when he placed [it] on the heart of his ox, the master is not concerned to remove it, since he will pay him the value of his ox. And Rabbeinu Tam explains that it was necessary [to teach] "a tied goat" that he is liable, even though we exempt concealed [items] in [damage by] fire — for we expound: "just as standing grain is in the open, so too everything [must be] in the open," and it might have entered our mind that anything whose nature is not so is not like standing grain and he is exempt, and a goat is not normally tied, so it might have entered our mind to exempt him — therefore [the Mishnah] now teaches us in the first clause that even so he is liable. And the latter clause teaches us that even though [the goat] is adjacent, which is in its normal manner, he is exempt. Therefore that Mishnah of [the chapter] HaKones (below, Bava Kamma 61b) is taught after the dispute concerning concealed [items] between R. Yehudah and the Rabbis; and after this clause of "a tied goat," it teaches: "And the Sages concede to R. Yehudah regarding one who sets fire to a large building, that he pays for everything that is inside it, for such is the way of people to place [things] in houses"; and the Tanna interrupted [between them] with this clause, as I have explained, to teach us that even though it is not the normal way for a goat to be tied, he is liable. And even according to the one who says "one's fire is [liable] because of his arrows" — for whom it is not relevant to exempt concealed [items] — nevertheless it was necessary to teach us that he is liable where his arrows were spent after the burning of the slave; and even though the burning of the slave is on account of his arrows and the burning of [the] goat is on account of his property, [the principle of] "he receives the greater penalty" applies to it well, since everything came about through one act. And know [that this is so], for according to the one who says [fire is liable] because of his property, he establishes [the Mishnah as referring to] when he set fire to the body of the slave, and we exempt him even though he did not set fire to the body of the goat. And according to the explanation of Rabbeinu Tam and Rashbam, it works out well why [the Mishnah] specifically mentioned a goat and did not [only] mention a stack of grain. And in the Kuntres [Rashi] he explained: because we conclude [that it refers to] one person's goat and another person's slave, whereas ordinarily the slave belongs to the owner of the stack of grain, for a person leaves his slave to guard his stack of grain; and according to his explanation, one must say [that] where [the Gemara] asks "Why was it necessary to state [this]?", it could have said: "And according to your reasoning, it should be a difficulty for R. Yochanan: why did [the Mishnah] mention a goat?"

Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:3:1.hebrew: קטל תוריה עבדא ה"נ דלא מיחייב - פ"ה: הא כתיב "כסף שלשים שקלים יתן לאדוניו". וקשה: דאם רצה לומר דה"ה לגבי אשו, דמשלם שלשים של עבד — הא אי אפשר לומר כן, דבפ"ק (דף ט:) אמרינן דהשור משלם שלשים של עבד, משא"כ באש! ואם ר"ל דכי היכי דהתם משלם קנס, ה"נ משלם דמי הגדי — הא לא גמרינן ממון מקנס! ונר' לר"י דהכי פריך: ה"נ דלא מחייב בממון שהזיק עם הריגת העבד? והא בדבר שממונו עושה לא שייך "קם ליה בדרבה מיניה":
Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:3:1.english: [If] his ox killed a slave, would he also not be liable - Rashi explains: Behold, it is written, "thirty shekels of silver he shall give to his master." And this is difficult: for if he meant to say that the same law applies regarding his fire, that he pays thirty [shekels] for a slave — behold, it is impossible to say so, for in the first chapter (9b) we say that an ox pays thirty [shekels] for a slave, which is not the case with fire! And if he meant to say that just as there he pays the fine, so too here he pays the value of the kid — behold, we do not derive monetary compensation from a fine! And it appears to Rabbeinu Yitzchak that this is what [the Gemara] is asking: Would he also not be liable for the property that it damaged along with the killing of the slave? Behold, with something that one's property does, [the principle of] "he is subject to the greater [penalty]" does not apply:

Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:5:1.hebrew: בגדי דחד ועבדא דחד - וכן נמי אמר רבא בפ' בן סורר ומורה (סנהדרין דף עד.): רודף שהיה רודף אחר חבירו להורגו ושיבר הכלים, בין של נרדף בין של כל אדם — פטור. וקשה, דבפ"ק דסנהדרין (דף י. ושם) אמר: ממון לזה ונפשות לזה — חייב! ותירץ הר"ר יצחק בר מרדכי, דכל רודף אחר חבירו חשיב מיתה ותשלומין לאחד, משום דמחייב מיתה לכל אדם, דהכל חייבין להורגו להציל הנרדף. ור"ת מפרש, דבכל מקום מיתה לזה ותשלומין לזה — פטור, לבד מעדים זוממין, דבעינן שיתקיים "כאשר זמם" בכל אחד; ואע"ג דבעדים זוממין נמי כשהוא מיתה ותשלומין לאחד פטור — התם משום דבההוא גברא מתקיים "כאשר זמם". והביא ראיה, דגמרינן (כתובות דף לה.) שאין מיתה ותשלומין מ"לא יהיה אסון ענש יענש" — הא אם יהיה אסון לא יענש, והתם מיתה לאשה ותשלומין לבעל. ומיהו אין זה ראיה, דעל כרחך צ"ל דהא חשיב מיתה ותשלומין לאחד, כיון שהן גוף אחד; דאי לאו הכי, למאי דבעי למימר מעיקרא בפ' בן סורר ומורה (סנהדרין דף עד.) גבי רודף, דמיתה לזה ותשלומין לזה חייב — היכי הוה משני ליה לקרא? ועוד הביא ראיה, דתנן במכילתין (דף לד:): דהוא שהדליק הגדיש או שחבל בחבירו בשבת — פטור, דקם ליה בדרבה מיניה, אע"ג דהוי מיתה לשמים ותשלומין לחבירו. ואין זה דיוקא, דזה חשיב מיתה ותשלומין לחד. וקצת קשה לר"י: מה חידוש יש בגדי דחד ועבדא דחד טפי ממה שהיה של אחד? הלא אין מתחייב מיתה לפי שהפסיד לו עבדו, דאפילו הרג עבד של עצמו — חייב! וצריך לדחוק, דמ"מ נ"ל חידוש יותר:
Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:5:1.english: Where the goat [belongs] to one [person] and the slave [belongs] to another - And so too Rava said in the chapter [entitled] Ben Sorer Umoreh (Sanhedrin 74a): A pursuer who was chasing after his fellow to kill him and broke utensils, whether [those] of the pursued or [those] of any [other] person, is exempt. And this is difficult, for in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (10a, and there [elsewhere]) it says: [Where] monetary [liability is] to this one and capital [liability is] to that one, he is liable! And Rabbi Yitzchak bar Mordechai answered that any pursuer [chasing] after his fellow is considered [a case of] death and payment to one [and the same party], because he is liable to death to everyone, since all are obligated to kill him to save the pursued. And Rabbeinu Tam explains that everywhere, [when] death [is] to this one and payment [is] to that one, he is exempt, except for conspiring witnesses, where we require that "as he conspired [to do]" be fulfilled with respect to each one; and even though with conspiring witnesses as well, when it is death and payment to one [person], he is exempt — there [it is] because with that [one] man "as he conspired [to do]" is fulfilled. And he brought a proof from [the fact] that we derive (Ketubot 35a) that there is no [combined] death and payment from "If there is no fatality, he shall surely be punished" — implying that if there is a fatality, he shall not be punished; and there, the death is to the woman and the payment is to the husband. However, this is not a proof, for perforce one must say that this is considered death and payment to one [party], since they are one body; for if not so, according to what [the Gemara] initially wanted to say in the chapter [entitled] Ben Sorer Umoreh (Sanhedrin 74a) regarding a pursuer, that [where] death is to this one and payment is to that one he is liable — how would it have answered the verse? And furthermore he brought a proof from what we learned in the Mishnah in our tractate (34b): that one who set fire to a stack of grain or injured his fellow on Shabbat is exempt, for he stands subject to the greater [penalty] (kam leih biderabbah mineih), even though the death [penalty] is to Heaven and the payment is to his fellow. Yet this is not an [accurate] inference, for this is considered death and payment to one [party]. And it is somewhat difficult for Ri: What greater novelty is there [in the case] where the goat [belongs] to one and the slave [belongs] to another than where [both] belonged to one [person]? After all, he does not incur the death penalty because he caused him the loss of his slave, for even if he killed his own slave he is liable! And one must force [an answer] that nevertheless it appears to me [to be] a greater novelty:

Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:7:1.hebrew: חציו דחרש הן - תימה לר"י: אי חשיב מסירה לחרש כרוח מצויה, לר' יוחנן נמי מחייב; ואי לא חשיב כרוח מצויה, א"כ מה קשה לר"ל? הא לא דמי למסר שורו, דהא כ"ע מודו דאין חייבין כלל על האש אלא ביכולה להזיק ברוח מצויה! ואומר ר"י, דלמ"ד אשו משום חציו, הוא לא מחייב אלא באש שיכול להזיק ברוח מצויה הרבה וקרוב לודאי היזק, כעין חציו; והכא אין במעשה השולח קרוב לודאי היזק, הלכך לא דמי לחציו, דחציו דחרש הן. אבל למ"ד משום ממונו, אע"ג דלא מזומן כולי האי, מחייב — מידי דהוי אמסר שורו קשור כראוי לחרש דחייב, דדרכו לנטורי ע"י עסקיו של חרש, אע"ג דלא הוי קרוב לודאי כעין חציו. והא דפוטר ר' יוחנן אפילו במסר לו שלהבת, לאו משום דאזיל לטעמיה דאית ליה אשו משום חציו — דהא מסיק דאית ליה נמי משום ממונו — אלא משום דקסבר שלהבת לא ברי הזיקא כמו שור, כדאמרינן בפרק קמא (דף ט:):
Tosafot on Bava Kamma 22b:7:1.english: They are the arrows of a deaf-mute - This is perplexing to the Ri: If handing [fire] over to a deaf-mute is considered like an ordinary wind, [then according to] R' Yochanan as well he should be liable; and if it is not considered like an ordinary wind, then what is the difficulty for Reish Lakish? For it is not comparable to one who hands over his ox, since everyone agrees that one is not liable at all for fire unless it is capable of causing damage in an ordinary wind! And the Ri says that according to the one who says [liability for] one's fire is due to [its being] his arrows, he is only liable for a fire that is capable of causing damage in a very common wind and where damage is nearly certain, similar to his arrows; and here, in the act of the one who sends [the fire], there is no near-certainty of damage, therefore it is not comparable to his arrows, for they are the arrows of the deaf-mute. However, according to the one who says [it is] due to his property, even though [the damage] is not so imminent, he is liable — just as in the case of one who hands over his properly tied ox to a deaf-mute, where he is liable, because it is usual for it to come untied through the actions of the deaf-mute, even though it is not near-certain like his arrows. And [as for] that which R' Yochanan exempts [him] even when he hands him a flame, it is not because he follows his own reasoning that he holds [liability for] one's fire is due to his arrows — for [the Gemara] concludes that he also holds [it is] due to his property — rather, it is because he holds that a flame's damage is not as certain as [that of] an ox, as we say in the first chapter (9b).
